# The Same Number on Your Air Quality App Could Be Four Different Kinds of Bad — Based on Where You Are

**What this piece covers, a quick summary:** The PM2.5 air quality
number on your phone is based on the weight of tiny particles in the
air. But weight alone turns out to be an incomplete guide to how harmful
those particles actually are. This piece explains four additional things
that matter beyond weight — how many particles there are, how much
surface area they present to your lungs, how chemically aggressive they
are, and what they are actually made of. It then walks through four
cities — Delhi, London, Beijing, and Los Angeles — each representing a
different pollution profile that the standard number cannot distinguish.
A glossary is at the end for quick reference while reading; a
limitations section and conclusion follow the city profiles.

**A note on terms:**

> Technical terms are defined in the glossary at the end of this piece.
> If you are reading this on a device where you can open two windows, it
> is worth keeping the glossary alongside — several terms (oxidative
> potential, alveoli, source apportionment) recur throughout. But, feel
> free to just start reading and refer when needed. The language is
> mostly intended for the general reader, so you don't need a background
> in AQ to understand most of the content below.

**A quick note before we go further:**

> Many apps show an **AQI — Air Quality Index** — rather than a raw
> PM2.5 number (usually in micrograms per cubic meter). AQI is a
> simplified scale (typically 0 to 500) that converts PM2.5
> concentration (one of the most harmful pollutants), along with other
> pollutants like ozone and nitrogen dioxide, into a single colour-coded
> score. It was designed for public communication, not scientific
> precision. The raw PM2.5 mass concentration number does a better job
> at more precisely communicating the true level of health harm, which
> can get lost in a general AQI score.
>
> Although, to assess health effects - looking at a raw PM2.5 mass
> concentration for a region is better than reading a general AQI - this
> raw PM2.5 mass still falls short of describing the actual level of
> potential health risks linked to these particles. This piece aims to
> discuss this gap and look at three other (other than mass) metrics:
> count, surface area and oxidative potential through which we can
> assess the quality of air around us in a more nuanced fashion.

## Background

Open your air quality app on a bad day in Delhi, London, Beijing, or Los
Angeles and you will see a number. Governments regulate it. Doctors cite
it. Millions of people check it every morning alongside the weather.

Whether your app shows "AQI: 150" or "PM2.5: 55 μg/m³", both numbers are
expressed as a mass concentration. But how that number was produced
varies — and this matters.

Reference-grade monitors measure mass directly by pulling air through a
filter and weighing the particles collected. This is slow, expensive,
and requires regular maintenance and laboratory analysis, which is why
reference monitors are relatively sparse — typically one or two per city
district, if that.

> **How consumer sensors work — and why it matters**
>
> The majority of readings people encounter in consumer apps and on air
> quality maps come from **low-cost sensors**, which use a different
> approach: an optical sensor shines a laser beam through the air,
> detects how particles scatter the light, and estimates mass
> concentration from those scattering events using a conversion formula.
> Low-cost sensors are transformative — they have made real-time air
> quality data accessible to millions of people, enabled dense urban
> monitoring networks that a handful of reference stations never could,
> and empowered communities to track local pollution in ways that were
> previously impossible. Their value is real and growing.
>
> What they measure is also genuinely different in one important way.
> The conversion from light scattering to mass concentration relies on
> assumptions about what the particles are like — their size, shape, and
> composition. In environments where those assumptions hold well,
> low-cost sensors perform closely to reference monitors. In
> environments where particle composition shifts significantly — during
> cooking smoke events, wildfires, or highly humid conditions, for
> example — the conversion can introduce uncertainty. This does not make
> low-cost sensor readings unreliable, but it is a reason to interpret
> them alongside their context rather than as absolute precision
> measurements.

Either way, the number both types of instrument produce is a mass-based
figure. And mass, as this piece explains, is not the whole story.

That number — PM2.5 at its core — is expressed as a mass concentration.
PM stands for particulate matter — airborne particles small enough to be
inhaled. The 2.5 refers to size, which I will explain properly in a
moment (see focus box below). The number is expressed in micrograms per
cubic meter: one microgram is one millionth of a gram, and a typical
grain of table salt weighs on the order of tens of micrograms (let's
assume 20 micrograms). One cubic meter is roughly the volume of a large
wardrobe. So a reading of 60 micrograms per cubic meter means that in
every wardrobe-sized volume of air around you, the total weight of all
floating particles together is comparable to the weight of a 3 grains of
salt. That sounds like almost nothing. The reason it matters is not how
heavy those particles are, but where they go when you breathe them in
and what they do when they get there.

Knowing this number is incredibly useful. But it is increasingly
recognised by researchers as a profound oversimplification — one that
makes four completely different chemical realities look equivalent. A
2024 study published in *Nature Communications*, drawing on 385 PM2.5
samples from 14 sites across four continents, found that the
relationship between PM2.5 mass and actual particle toxicity is "largely
non-linear due to significant differences in the intrinsic toxicity" of
particles from different locations [1]. In plain language: the same
number can represent very different dangers depending on where you are
standing and what is burning nearby.

To understand why, you need four ways of measuring the same air — not
just one.

A controlled clinical trial published in *npj Clean Air* in May 2026
makes this concrete in a way that large-scale epidemiology — the study
of health patterns across whole populations — cannot [22]. Researchers
at the University of Manchester exposed 15 healthy volunteers, each aged
over 50 with a family history of dementia, to four different pollution
sources inside a precisely controlled chamber: woodsmoke, diesel
exhaust, cooking emissions, and limonene secondary organic aerosol — a
type of particle formed when limonene, a chemical found in many cleaning
products and air fresheners, reacts with other compounds in indoor air.

Crucially, the PM2.5 mass concentration was standardised to the same
target across all four exposures. Same particle mass. Different sources
— and, as the authors note, different co-emitted gases that could not be
controlled, because real-world combustion sources produce them in fixed
ratios alongside particles.

The results differed. NOX concentrations were substantially higher in
the diesel and woodsmoke conditions than in cooking emissions or
limonene SOA. Diesel exhaust showed a trend toward worse performance on
a test of focused attention. Woodsmoke and limonene SOA were associated
with reduced lung function compared to clean air, even after just 60
minutes of exposure. Woodsmoke and diesel exhaust were linked to faster
basic reaction times. The authors caution that this may be driven by
nitric oxide — a gas released alongside these pollutants — which can
dilate blood vessels and briefly alter brain blood flow, rather than
indicating any genuinely positive or beneficial effect of exposure.

The authors concluded that "specific pollutant sources acutely
influenced cognition and lung function, with responses varying by
source" [22].

The trial had only 13 participants who completed all visits — a small
number for a health study — and the authors present it as an early-stage
demonstration of the method rather than definitive clinical proof. The
inability to control co-emitted gases means particle effects cannot be
cleanly separated from gas-phase effects in this study, which the
authors acknowledge.

But, all that aside - as a demonstration that the same PM2.5 mass target
from different real-world sources produces measurably different
biological outcomes in the similar people — whether driven by particles,
gases, or their interaction — it is unusually direct evidence that the
single number does not capture what the body actually experiences.

## Four Ways to Measure the Same Air

Before comparing four ways to measure air pollution, it helps to be
clear about what the current dominant way (micrograms per cubic meter)
and its underlying unit - "mass" actually means — because everything
else in this piece is a contrast to it.

> **Mass and weight — a minor, but important distinction to keep in
> mind**
>
> Mass and weight are often used interchangeably in everyday life, but
> they are different things. **Mass** is the amount of physical matter
> something contains — it does not change wherever you are. **Weight**
> is the force that gravity exerts on that mass — it would be slightly
> different on the Moon.
>
> In air quality measurement, this distinction rarely matters in
> practice but is useful to keep in mind. Monitors effectively weigh
> particles collected on a filter and, because gravity is constant,
> report this as mass. So when PM2.5 is described as a mass-based
> metric, it refers to the amount of material present, which can
> effectively be interpreted as weight. But, aspects such as particle
> count, surface area, oxidative potential, and chemical composition are
> not captured by mass/weight. We use mass and weight interchangeably in
> this post, as the distinction does not affect the discussion in
> practice.

When reference-grade air quality monitors measure PM2.5, they pull air
through a filter over a period of time, then weigh the filter before and
after. The difference is the mass of particles caught. This is the gold
standard — slow and laboratory-grade, but precise.

Mass is a useful and real measurement. But notice what it does not tell
you. Weighing a bag of flour tells you nothing about how many individual
grains there are, how much combined surface area those grains present,
or whether the flour is ordinary or coated in something harmful. A bag
of a hundred large lumps and a bag of ten million fine grains can weigh
exactly the same. The scale reports one number. The contents are not the
same thing.

That is the starting point. Now here are four ways to look at the same
air.

To understand this, let's picture a jar containing a dozen large
marbles, 2 or 3 small pebbles, and ten million grains of sand.

You could describe the contents in four different ways, each revealing
something the others hide.

**Mass/Weight — what we currently measure**

Put the jar on a scale. The marbles dominate. They are so much heavier
individually that the sand barely registers (relatively), even though
there are ten million grains of it. The scale gives you one number that
mainly reflects the marbles. You know something is there. You do not
know how many individual objects, how much combined surface area they
have, or how harmful each type might be.

This is the PM2.5 reading. It measures the total mass of airborne
particles in a given volume of air by pulling air through a filter and
weighing what gets caught.

**Count — how many individual particles**

Count every object in the jar individually. The ten million grains of
sand overwhelm everything else entirely. The same jar looks completely
different described by count rather than weight. In the lungs, more
individual particles means more separate events — more sites where a
particle lands, more locations where a biological response can be
triggered, regardless of how little each particle weighs.

**Surface area — how much combined exterior**

Calculate the total exterior surface of everything in the jar. When
particles differ substantially in size — as for e.g. ultrafine particles
do compared to larger PM2.5 particles (or PM2.5 relative to PM10) — the
smaller ones have dramatically more combined surface area for the same
total weight.

> **For the curious, a sidebar: why surface area scales differently from
> mass**
>
> Think of a particle as a tiny sphere. A sphere has two relevant
> measurements: its surface — the outside skin — and its volume — the
> space it fills inside.
>
> Start with surface area. Imagine looking at a sphere straight on —
> what you see is a circle. The area of that circle depends on the
> radius squared. Double the diameter of the sphere and the circle you
> see quadruples in area. That is what "surface area scales with the
> square of the diameter" means in plain terms: make a sphere twice as
> wide and its surface area becomes four times larger, not two times.
>
> Now think about volume — how much space the sphere fills. If you
> double the diameter, every dimension of the sphere doubles at the same
> time. Volume depends on three dimensions — width, height, and depth —
> so doubling each of them multiplies the total space by two times two
> times two. That equals eight. So doubling the diameter does not just
> double the volume — it makes it eight times larger. That is what
> “volume scales with the cube of the diameter” means: increase the size
> in all directions, and the total space — and therefore the mass —
> grows much faster.
>
> Now put those two facts together. Double the diameter: surface area
> goes up by four, mass goes up by eight. So mass grew twice as fast as
> surface area. Run this in reverse for smaller particles: halve the
> diameter and mass drops to one-eighth, but surface area only drops to
> one-quarter. That means the smaller particle now has twice as much
> surface area relative to its mass as the original larger one.
>
> Repeat this logic across millions of ultrafine particles — each one a
> fraction of the size of a PM2.5 particle — and the combined surface
> area becomes very large relative to their combined weight. Far larger
> than the same weight of bigger particles would produce.

Think of the difference between a block of salt and the same weight of
salt ground into fine crystals. Both contain the same amount of
material, but the smaller crystals expose far more total surface area to
the water, so they dissolve much faster. It is this increase in surface
area that drives the effect. In the lungs, something similar happens:
for the same mass, smaller particles collectively present much more
surface area, creating more points of contact with tissue and allowing
interactions to happen more quickly.

**Oxidative potential — how chemically aggressive those surfaces are**

The sand in one version of the jar is ordinary beach sand. In another,
it is coated in a reactive chemical. Same weight. Same count. Same
surface area. Completely different danger.

**Oxidative potential** is the capacity of a particle to generate
reactive oxygen species, or ROS. You can think of these as tiny chemical
sparks produced when certain particles interact with biological tissue —
either directly or by triggering cells to produce them. These highly
reactive molecules can attack cell membranes, proteins, and DNA — like a
slow internal rusting process applied to living tissue rather than an
iron pipe. Over time, if this oxidative stress overwhelms the body’s
defenses, it can damage the cell’s basic machinery: membranes can become
leaky, proteins can misfold, and DNA can accumulate oxidative lesions or
strand breaks, increasing the risk of errors during replication. The
capacity of a particle to produce ROS varies enormously: near-zero for
something like sea salt, very high for particles coated in combustion
products, certain metals, or organic compounds from burning fuel.
Research increasingly describes oxidative potential as a more
health-relevant metric than mass concentration, precisely because mass
can contain a mix of components ranging from highly toxic to relatively
benign [5] — and the scale cannot tell them apart.

The PM2.5 number on your app is the jar on the scale. Accurate.
Standardised and very useful, yet systematically blind to other
important aspects such as count, surface area, and what coats each
particle (which help determines the oxidative potential of the
particle).

> **Sidebar (feel free to skip if you are familiar with what PM2.5
> means): What Does "2.5" Actually Mean? - A deeper dive**
>
> The 2.5 is a size threshold. Particles smaller than 2.5 micrometers in
> diameter get counted in the measurement. Larger ones do not. These
> particles are made up of organics, soot (black carbon), inorganic
> salts (like sulfates and nitrates), metals, and dust, with composition
> varying by source.
>
> To get a sense of scale: a PM2.5 particle at the threshold is roughly
> the size of a bacterium — something so small it was invisible to
> humans until the invention of the microscope. A human hair is about 50
> to 70 micrometers wide, meaning you could line up around 25 of these
> particles across a single strand's width. You could inhale millions of
> these harmful particles in a single breath.
>
> The reason this particular threshold matters is straightforward:
> smaller particles travel deeper into the lungs. Larger particles get
> trapped in the nose and throat before reaching vulnerable tissue.
> Particles smaller than 2.5 micrometers in diameter make it all the way
> to the deepest part of the lungs — and the smallest among them, reach
> the alveolar region, where oxygen crosses from air into the
> bloodstream. This is why scientists and regulators settled on this
> cutoff. But, in general the smaller the particle gets the more deeper
> inside the body it can easily reach.
>
> Think of it like a sieve. A sieve does not care what shape something
> is, what it is made of, or how heavy it is — it only asks one
> question: is it small enough to pass through the mesh? Anything that
> passes through gets counted. Anything too big gets caught. PM2.5 works
> the same way — it captures all particles whose diameter is below 2.5
> micrometers, regardless of what they are made of, how many there are,
> or how reactive their surfaces are - they all count as PM2.5. A
> particle of sea salt and a particle of arsenic-coated soot both pass
> through if they are small enough. The sieve cannot tell their chemical
> nature apart.
>
> The sieve also has one imperfection worth knowing about. The cutoff is
> not perfectly sharp — some particles slightly above 2.5 micrometers in
> diameter slip through and get counted anyway [2]. This matters because
> bigger particles are much heavier — doubling a particle's diameter
> makes it eight times heavier, because mass scales with volume and
> volume grows as the cube of the diameter. So even a small number of
> slightly oversized particles can contribute disproportionately to the
> final weight reading.
>
> Which brings us to the deeper issue. Whatever passes through the sieve
> gets weighed. And weight is dominated by the biggest, heaviest
> particles in the sample. The tiny particles do contribute to the total
> weight — but because they weigh almost nothing individually, their
> combined contribution is dwarfed by a much smaller number of heavier
> particles. A few heavy particles can outweigh millions of tiny ones on
> the scale. So the final number ends up reflecting the heavy end of
> what passed through far more than the tiny end — even if the tiny
> particles are present in vastly greater numbers and may pose more
> health risk. We'll explore this further below.

With those four lenses established and the meaning of "2.5" clarified,
it is worth pausing to ask: if these nuances are real, why does the
standard number ignore them?

PM2.5 mass measurement was a genuine scientific advance when introduced
in the 1990s, replacing a focus on coarser, less health-relevant
particles with one grounded in evidence about how fine particles affect
the lungs. It has contributed to substantial health improvements in
regulated regions. At the same time, the metric relies on what was then
(and continues to be) a practical and robust method—collecting particles
on a filter and weighing them—which captures total mass but not the full
range of biologically relevant properties. But, as monitoring
technologies and toxicological insights have advanced, it has become
clearer that mass alone cannot distinguish between more and less harmful
particle mixtures. The four cities below are where that limitation
becomes visible in human terms.

One important framing note before the cities begin. Each city is
presented because it illustrates a particular pollution profile most
clearly — but these profiles are not unique to these cities. Biomass and
combustion-dominated pollution like Delhi's exists across much of South
and Southeast Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, and anywhere biomass burning and
older vehicles predominate. Traffic-dominated aging particle profiles
like London's characterise many dense European and North American
cities. Coal-sourced heavy metal loading like Beijing's is the story of
many industrial cities in China, Eastern Europe, and parts of the Middle
East. Wildfire-driven complex chemical exposures like Los Angeles's are
increasingly the story of western North America, southern Europe, and
Australia. The cities are entry points into recognisable pollution
types, not exceptional cases.

***Note on interpreting the city wise sections below:***

> The city narratives that follow are illustrative, not exhaustive. They
> highlight pollution patterns that are commonly observed in each
> location, but real-world conditions are often more complex and can
> vary across time, neighborhoods, and sources.
>
> These examples are drawn from general pollution profiles, but they are
> not meant to suggest that such patterns are unique to one city or
> absent in others. Similar processes—such as particle transformation,
> source mixing, and exposure differences—can occur across urban
> environments worldwide.
>
> The goal is not to define each city rigidly, but to use them as
> concrete examples to understand a broader point: that the same PM2.5
> mass concentration can arise from very different pollution profiles,
> and those differences can lead to very different health consequences.

## Delhi — A City Where Every Combustion Source Burns at Once

*Most characteristic profile: biomass, vehicle exhaust, and residential
burning layered simultaneously, trapped by geography*

It is early morning in Delhi in January. The nights have been cold —
temperatures dropping to around 8 to 10 degrees Celsius before dawn, the
kind of cold that sends millions of households across the city reaching
for whatever fuel is available: wood, pressed agricultural waste, crop
residue. On the main roads, vehicles start up in the chill. In the
surrounding states, farmers are burning the rice-paddy stubble left from
harvest before the wheat planting begins. All of this happens
simultaneously, across one of the most densely populated flatlands on
earth.

A monitor records the PM2.5 mass concentration. The reading is very high
— Delhi's winter air consistently far exceeds WHO guidelines [3]. But
the mass reading by itself does not answer the important question: what
is actually in that number, and how harmful is it?

**Mass:** High and roughly uniform across the entire region — whether
inside Delhi or in the surrounding agricultural belt. The monitor's
reading accurately reflects severity. But it treats all particles
equally.

**Count and surface area:** The particles dominating count and surface
area are very small — organic aerosols produced when fuel burns
incompletely. Small particles reach the deepest, most vulnerable part of
the lungs and into the bloodstream in large numbers.

> To understand why size matters so much here, consider how the
> respiratory system defends itself.
>
> The nose and upper throat trap large particles in mucus. Further down,
> the airways are lined with millions of microscopic hair-like
> structures called **cilia** that beat in coordinated waves, moving a
> thin layer of mucus upward like a slow conveyor belt — the
> **mucociliary escalator**. Particles trapped in this mucus get swept
> upward and out. This defence works well for particles larger than
> about 2.5 micrometers.
>
> Smaller particles slip past entirely. They reach the **alveoli**:
> roughly 300 million tiny air sacs packed into the deepest part of the
> lungs, where oxygen passes from air into the bloodstream and carbon
> dioxide passes back out. Alveolar walls are only one cell thick —
> necessarily, because that thinness allows gas exchange. There are no
> cilia here. And critically, PM2.5 particles that reach the alveoli do
> not simply sit there: PM2.5 can cross tinto the bloodstream directly,
> from where they are carried to secondary organs — the heart, liver,
> brain — well beyond the lung itself.

The combustion particles are exactly the size range that reaches the
alveoli and, in part, passes beyond them. They arrive in enormous
numbers per breath, presenting large combined surface area against
tissue that has very limited defences.

**Oxidative potential:** A 2024 study in *Nature Communications*
examined PM2.5 at five sites inside and outside Delhi, chemically
fingerprinting the particles to trace them back to their sources and
measuring their oxidative potential [4].\
\
The study found this was overwhelmingly driven by organic aerosols from
incomplete combustion, whether from traffic, household heating, or
agricultural burning. The ammonium sulfate and nitrate particles found
in higher proportions outside Delhi — formed when agricultural ammonia
reacts with acidic gases in the atmosphere rather than from direct
combustion — had much lower oxidative potential despite contributing
similar mass to the reading. Same mass number. Substantially different
chemical aggression in the body.

**Chemical composition:** Delhi's combustion particles carry **PAHs —
polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons** — a family of organic compounds that
form whenever any carbon-containing material burns incompletely. This is
not unique to Delhi: it happens in car engines, open fires, coal
furnaces, and agricultural burning worldwide. Several PAHs are
classified as confirmed human carcinogens. When the body tries to break
PAHs down, the process produces reactive intermediates that bind
directly to DNA, damaging it in ways that can contribute to cancer over
time. Research reviewing lung cancer in people who have never smoked
identifies combustion-related indoor air pollution as an associated risk
factor for lung cancer, with oxidative stress and DNA damage in lung
tissue as the proposed biological mechanism — though separating the
specific contribution of PAHs from the many other harmful compounds in
combustion smoke is genuinely difficult to do in research, and has not
been fully resolved [6].

The weight reading tells you Delhi's air is severely polluted. This
alone is concerning. But, on top of that the other four dimensions help
explain why it can be so much more concerning then what it appears to
be.

## London — Where the Measurement-Exposure Gap becomes Visible

*Most characteristic profile: combustion particles that transform
between emission and measurement, creating a hidden exposure gap near
busy roads — with traffic no longer the only significant source*

London's busy main roads at rush hour look nothing like Delhi. No
visible smoke. PM2.5 readings within ranges that European regulations
consider borderline acceptable.

But something important happens to particles in the seconds and metres
between a vehicle exhaust pipe and the nearest air quality monitor,
which may be several hundred metres away. They age — and in ageing, they
change across all four dimensions simultaneously.

**Count:** Fresh diesel exhaust produces **ultrafine particles** —
particles smaller than 0.1 micrometers, so individually light that they
contribute almost nothing to PM2.5 mass, but enormous in number. Within
seconds of emission, these particles collide with each other and stick
together, forming **agglomerates**: clusters of many small particles
fused into single larger ones, like individual specks of dust clumping
into a visible flake. Each agglomeration event replaces many small
particles with one larger one. Particle count drops substantially as air
travels away from the source.

**Surface area:** A large agglomerate has less total exterior surface
than the many small particles it assembled from — just as a snowball has
less combined surface than all the individual snowflakes compressed
inside it. As particles age and agglomerate, surface area per unit of
mass falls. Someone breathing air directly near a vehicle exhaust is
exposed to far more particle surface area per microgram than what the
distant monitor captures (by when smaller particles have combined to
make agglomerates).

**Mass:** Each agglomerate is heavier than its component particles
individually, so mass per particle rises even as count drops. By the
time aged air reaches the monitor, the mass reading is reasonably
representative of that air — but not of what someone breathing 20 metres
from a bus is inhaling.

**Oxidative potential:** Freshly formed combustion particles have
chemically reactive surfaces that have not yet stabilised. As particles
age, their surfaces oxidise and become less reactive. The monitor
several hundred metres away captures older, calmer particles. The person
near the exhaust pipe inhales fresher, more reactive ones — higher
oxidative potential per particle than what the monitor records.

What does this gap actually mean for health? A randomised controlled
study published in *The Lancet* had participants — including people with
chronic lung disease and heart disease — walk for two hours either along
Oxford Street, one of central London's busiest shopping streets with
heavy traffic, or through Hyde Park nearby [7]. The researchers measured
**black carbon** (the elemental soot core of diesel combustion particles
— a marker of how fresh and traffic-related the exposure is), nitrogen
dioxide, PM2.5, and ultrafine particle counts at both locations.

Oxford Street had substantially higher levels of all of these.

-   People with chronic lung disease reported significantly more wheeze,
    cough, and breathlessness after the Oxford Street walk.
-   Across all participants, including healthy volunteers, walking in
    Hyde Park was associated with improved lung function and reduced
    **arterial stiffness** — a measure of how hard the heart must work
    to pump blood through the arteries; stiffer arteries mean greater
    cardiovascular strain over time.
-   Walking on Oxford Street was associated with attenuated improvements
    in both lung function and arterial stiffness.
-   These differences persisted when measured 26 hours later [7].

One walk. Two hours. Measurable in the body the next day. This does not
mean a single walk causes heart disease — cardiovascular disease
develops over years of repeated exposure. What the study demonstrates is
that the biological processes involved in cardiovascular stress are
already being activated at levels of short-term exposure that the nearby
PM2.5 monitor did not fully capture.

> **Chemical composition and long-term evidence:** London's black carbon
> profile has shifted significantly over the past decade. Traffic was
> historically the dominant source — a pattern well-documented in
> measurements taken before 2015. But London's Ultra Low Emission Zone,
> introduced in 2019 and expanded city-wide in 2023, has substantially
> reduced exhaust emissions from older diesel vehicles. A 2025
> peer-reviewed study measuring black carbon fluxes from the BT Tower in
> central London found that non-road mobile machinery — generators and
> heavy equipment on construction sites — can now dominate over vehicle
> traffic as a black carbon source in areas with dense building activity
> [23]. This is a finding specific to central London's
> high-construction-density areas rather than a citywide conclusion, and
> it is the first study of its kind in Europe. The broader picture for
> London is that black carbon now comes from a more mixed set of
> combustion sources than it did a decade ago, with construction,
> residential wood burning, and residual traffic all contributing
> alongside each other.
>
> The short-term health evidence from traffic exposure remains clear and
> is not undermined by this shift: a study examining daily black carbon
> levels and hospital admissions in London found consistent associations
> between elemental carbon and adult cardiovascular admissions, as well
> as paediatric respiratory admissions, independently of other
> pollutants measured simultaneously [9]. The particle ageing physics
> described above — fresh reactive particles near any combustion source,
> calmer aged particles at the distant monitor — applies whether the
> source is a bus or a diesel generator.
>
> For long-term effects, the picture is more complex and worth being
> explicit about. A cohort study — one that follows a large group of
> people over many years and tracks who develops disease — is the
> standard tool for this kind of question. A London-specific study
> tracking over 211,000 adults found the strongest associations between
> traffic-related air pollution and heart failure, while associations
> with other cardiovascular outcomes were harder to detect [19]. This is
> not evidence that pollution is safe in London — it reflects the
> genuine statistical difficulty of isolating traffic-specific effects
> at the relatively lower pollution concentrations found in a European
> city, where multiple pollutants move together and other health risk
> factors complicate the picture. The evidence strengthens considerably
> when looking across multiple European populations: the ELAPSE study,
> which pooled data from six European cohort studies, found significant
> associations between long-term black carbon exposure and stroke, at
> concentrations below existing EU and WHO guideline limits [21]. A
> separate British cohort study with over 25 years of follow-up found
> associations between air pollution and cardiovascular mortality [20].

The honest picture for London is this: the short-term biological effects
of traffic pollution on cardiovascular function are well-documented. The
long-term evidence from population studies for black carbon specifically
driving cardiovascular disease in lower-pollution European settings is
suggestive and consistent with what we know about the biological
mechanisms, but still less definitive than the evidence for PM2.5 in
higher-pollution settings. This does not mean the concern is unfounded —
it means the science is appropriately uncertain at the margins, and that
uncertainty is itself worth knowing. More research will further guide
the way.

## Beijing — When Coal Declined, the Air Told a Different Story

*Most characteristic profile: a city that was coal-dominated until
recently — and whose dramatic improvement shows exactly why composition
monitoring matters more than mass monitoring alone*

Beijing in winter was, for much of the 2000s and 2010s, one of the most
severely polluted cities on earth. In the worst haze episodes the PM2.5
readings were extreme — visibility dropped to a few city blocks, the
skyline disappeared into yellow-brown murk, and there was sometimes a
metallic taste in the air. That picture has changed substantially.
China's coal controls began with the Air Pollution Prevention and
Control Action Plan launched in 2013, which set binding PM2.5 reduction
targets for Beijing and mandated coal substitution with natural gas and
electricity. These were intensified through the Three-Year Action Plan
for Winning the Blue Sky War from 2018. Together these policies have
driven significant reductions in Beijing's PM2.5. Peer-reviewed research
published in 2023 found that coal combustion is no longer an important
contributor to PM2.5 in Beijing city itself, with secondary aerosol
formation and biomass burning now the dominant sources [24]. Beijing's
air quality story has genuinely improved.

But Beijing is included here not as a current warning but as the
clearest available demonstration of why composition monitoring matters —
because it was composition data, not just mass measurements, that
revealed what was causing harm and confirmed what the coal ban was
fixing.

> **How source apportionment works**
>
> **Source apportionment** is the scientific practice of chemically
> fingerprinting pollutants, e.g. PM2.5 to identify what fraction came
> from which emission source. Different combustion processes leave
> different chemical fingerprints in the particles they produce: coal
> burning deposits characteristic metals and sulfate compounds; diesel
> exhaust leaves a black carbon and organic compound signature; biomass
> burning releases elevated potassium — a marker that shows up reliably
> in smoke from burning plant material; industrial smelting leaves its
> own distinctive metal combinations. By analysing the full chemical
> composition of PM2.5 samples, researchers can work backwards to
> identify what fraction of the pollution came from coal, traffic,
> agriculture, or industry — and crucially, which sources drive the most
> harmful particle types.

**Mass, count, and surface area:** During the coal-dominated years,
Beijing's winter PM2.5 was heavily influenced by coal combustion
particles, which have a somewhat broader size distribution than fresh
diesel exhaust or biomass fires. The particles tended to be heavier
individually, which meant the PM2.5 mass reading was quite
representative of the total particle burden. Count and surface area were
substantial — but neither is the most distinctive feature of Beijing's
pollution story.

**Oxidative potential:** High during heavy pollution episodes, driven by
combustion organics and certain metals — particularly iron, copper, and
manganese, which are known to generate reactive oxygen species. But
again, not the most distinctive dimension. Oxidative potential depends
on chemical composition (see below) because it is driven by reactive
components like certain metals and organics, so major compositional
changes can shift it. However, it is not a one-to-one reflection of
composition, since interactions between components can amplify or
suppress overall reactivity

**Chemical composition — what the historical data revealed:** A health
risk assessment of Beijing PM2.5 samples collected between 2013 and 2015
— during the height of the coal-dominated period — found that arsenic
carried the highest modelled individual cancer risk of any measured
component, exceeding the internationally accepted risk threshold [10].
The word "modelled" is worth noting: this is a calculated risk based on
measured concentrations and established toxicological risk factors, not
a direct count of cancer cases traceable to these particles. That said,
the methodology is standard in environmental health risk assessment and
the findings are consistent with the broader literature. Arsenic,
cadmium, chromium, lead, and nickel — all classified as human
carcinogens — were found at concentrations traceable primarily to coal
combustion and road dust during that period. Coal combustion in winter
drove the majority of heavy metal loading and the associated modelled
cancer risk [10].

This is the story the mass number could not tell.

Arsenic is associated with bladder and kidney cancer. Cadmium is
associated with kidney damage and lung cancer. These are not pollutants
that remain localised at the point where particles land in the lung — as
with PM2.5 more broadly, they are absorbed into the bloodstream and
distributed throughout the body, accumulating in organs far from where
inhalation occurred. This is most clearly documented in workers with
very high occupational exposures — miners and smelter workers — but the
same basic mechanism applies at lower environmental concentrations, even
if the precise relationship between exposure level and health effect at
those lower concentrations is less completely mapped.

Consider a concrete illustration of what the mass number cannot
distinguish. Two people in two different cities both check their apps
and see a reading of 75 micrograms per cubic meter — a concerning level
by any standard. Person A is in a coal-heavy city breathing coal
combustion particles carrying arsenic and cadmium. Person B is in a
rural agricultural region of Europe where the PM2.5 is dominated by
ammonium sulfate and ammonium nitrate — secondary particles formed when
ammonia from livestock and fertilisers reacts with acidic gases in the
atmosphere, chemically inert, contributing substantially to mass but
carrying relatively low oxidative potential and no heavy metals. Both
apps show 75. Person A is being exposed to confirmed carcinogens that
distribute beyond the lung. Person B is not. The instrument cannot
distinguish them.

**Why this is actually a story about what good monitoring can do:** When
the Chinese government implemented strict coal combustion controls from
2013 onward, researchers tracked not just PM2.5 mass but the detailed
chemical composition of what was in the air. Research comparing heavy
metal concentrations in PM2.5 across Chinese cities before and after
China's 2018 air quality action plan found that concentrations of
arsenic, cadmium, and related metals declined substantially in the
post-2018 period compared to 2014–2018, consistent with coal reduction
[11]. More recent research confirms that coal combustion is no longer a
dominant primary source in Beijing city itself [24]. The mass reading
told Beijing its air was improving. The composition data told it which
organs were becoming safer, confirmed what the intervention was actually
achieving, and provided the evidence base to show the coal ban worked.
That precision is what mass monitoring alone could never have provided —
and it is the same precision that would be available to every city, for
every pollution source, if composition monitoring were routine rather
than exceptional.

## Los Angeles — When the Suburbs Burn

*Most characteristic profile: wildfire smoke, increasingly from fires
burning through built-up areas, releasing chemical compounds no prior
air quality framework anticipated*

Los Angeles sits at the intersection of two wildfire problems that are
often conflated but are meaningfully different.

The first is the familiar one: forest and shrubland fires burning
vegetation in the hills and mountains surrounding the city, sending
large plumes of PM2.5 downwind. This has characterised California's fire
seasons for decades, and the health burden is substantial. A modelling
study estimated that wildfire PM2.5 smoke in California between 2008 and
2018 — is estimated to have contributed to a total of 52,480 to 55,710
premature deaths over the 11-year period, equating to an economic impact
of \$432 to \$456 billion[25].

The second problem is newer and in some respects more concerning: the
**wildland-urban interface fire**, or WUI fire. These are fires that
begin in vegetation but spread into built-up neighbourhoods, burning
houses, vehicles, and consumer goods alongside trees and grass. As
residential development has expanded into fire-prone areas around
California's cities, WUI fires have increased markedly: research found a
more than fourfold increase in conditions conducive to extreme-impact
WUI fires in California from 1990 to 2022 [18]. A report from the
California Council on Science and Technology noted that smoke from WUI
fires — combining burning buildings with burning biomass — was
associated with substantially greater health risk than smoke from
wildland-only fires [17].

The distinction matters because what burns determines what is in the
smoke. And in a suburb, almost everything that burns was not designed
with combustion in mind.

Here is how WUI fire smoke compares across the four dimensions:

**Count:** Fresh wildfire smoke is dominated by ultrafine particles,
enormous in number and chemically reactive, with high surface area per
unit of mass [13]. Unlike London's aged diesel particles, these have not
had time to agglomerate and stabilise. They arrive at the alveoli in a
freshly reactive state.

**Surface area:** Higher per unit of mass than almost any other common
outdoor pollution scenario, because the particles are small and freshly
emitted in huge numbers.

**Mass:** Can spike to extreme levels during active fires, rivalling the
worst pollution episodes in other cities. The mass number here
accurately reflects acute severity.

**Oxidative potential:** High, driven by fresh reactive particle
surfaces. But oxidative potential does not capture everything harmful in
WUI smoke — because some of the most concerning components act through
entirely different biological pathways.

**Chemical composition:** A field sampling study of the January 2025 Los
Angeles fires found that standard PM2.5 mass measurements "may
underestimate the toxicological burden" of such events [14]. The
researchers documented elevated concentrations of PAHs, non-crustal
metals (metals not from soil or rock, meaning they came from
manufactured objects: electronics, vehicles, building materials), BTEX
compounds — benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylene, a group of
volatile toxic chemicals released from burning synthetic materials,
several of which are confirmed or probable human carcinogens — and PFAS
compounds.

Wildfire smoke from burning vegetation and structures also generates
**secondary organic aerosol (SOA)** — particles formed in the atmosphere
when gases released during combustion react with each other to create
new compounds that were not present in the original emissions. SOA from
limonene, a compound released by burning vegetation and wood products,
is one example. The HIPTox trial found that limonene SOA was associated
with reduced lung function in healthy volunteers after 60 minutes of
standardised exposure [22] — a finding that, while preliminary given the
small sample, points toward health effects from particle types that
outdoor monitoring systems are not designed to detect.

> **PFAS in wildfire smoke — a plausible concern, not yet a settled
> risk**
>
> **PFAS — per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances** — are a large family of
> synthetic chemicals used in non-stick cookware coatings, waterproof
> clothing, food packaging, carpet treatments, and firefighting foam.
> They are sometimes called "forever chemicals" because the
> carbon-fluorine bond that makes them useful is one of the strongest in
> chemistry, making them extraordinarily resistant to breaking down in
> the environment or inside the human body.
>
> When a suburban house burns, every PFAS-containing product in it
> releases these compounds into the smoke, where they attach to
> particles and are inhaled [14]. A 2024 review of PFAS lung health
> effects found associations with impaired fetal lung development,
> reduced immune function in children, and potential carcinogenicity
> through inhalation [15]. These associations come largely from large
> population studies and animal research. The specific health effects of
> inhaling PFAS-bearing wildfire smoke particles — as distinct from
> other routes of PFAS exposure such as drinking water — are not yet
> well-characterised.
>
> What is established is that PFAS compounds act through mechanisms —
> disrupting the immune system, interfering with hormone signalling,
> accumulating persistently in body tissues — that are entirely
> different from the reactive oxygen species pathway that dominates
> combustion particle research. An oxidative potential measurement does
> not detect PFAS toxicity. The concern is legitimate and warrants
> research. It is not yet an established inhalation risk in the way that
> diesel exhaust or arsenic exposure is, and should be understood
> accordingly.

The LA PM2.5 number reported elevated particulate levels. It had no
mechanism to communicate that some of what was being inhaled had no
established place in any prior air quality framework.

## An Important Clarification

> ***We have been discussing how mass concentration captures only one
> aspect of the measurement story. But, I should note it clearly that
> mass concentration is a very important and extremely useful aspect and
> we will continue to use it. But, the piece aims at directing attention
> to other less discussed aspects, which should also become part of
> mainstream discussions as they are equally (if not more) important.***

Mass concentration correlates with harm well enough that decades of
research have established air pollution as associated with approximately
7.9 million premature deaths per year globally [16]. That correlation is
real, hard-won, and has driven genuine improvements in public health in
cities that have reduced pollution. Reducing PM2.5 mass saves lives. No
denying that. But as discussed in this post, "in addition" to this we
need to keep the following in mind:

A 2024 study drawing on samples from 14 sites across four continents
found, however, that the relationship between PM2.5 mass and actual
toxicity is largely non-linear globally — meaning reducing mass does not
necessarily reduce harm proportionally if the most toxic fractions
remain [1].

The argument is more precise: mass concentration tells you *how much* is
in the air. It cannot tell you *what* it is, *where it goes* in the
body, *what it does* when it gets there, or *where it came from*. Count,
surface area, oxidative potential, and chemical composition are not
academic refinements.

They are the questions that explain why identical mass readings in
different cities produce different disease burdens, why the person near
traffic breathes something the distant monitor did not capture, why
Beijing's coal reduction improved health in organs the mass number
cannot see, and why WUI wildfire smoke carries hazards that existing
frameworks had not anticipated.

## The Technology Is Moving — at Different Speeds for Each Metric

The four metrics described in this piece are not hypothetical —
instruments for measuring count, surface area, and oxidative potential
already exist. What varies is how far each has travelled from research
laboratory toward routine monitoring.

**Particle count** is closest to deployment. Field-ready instruments now
exist — QuantAQ launched the MODULAIR-UFP in May 2025, a condensation
particle counter designed for continuous outdoor deployment [26]. More
significantly, EU Directive 2024/2881, which entered into force in
December 2024, requires all member states to monitor ultrafine particle
number concentrations, with dedicated monitoring stations where particle
number and size distribution must be measured continuously [27, 28].

**Oxidative potential** has moved from laboratory to field deployment.
Multiple independent research groups have developed instruments that
continuously collect ambient PM2.5 and measure its oxidative activity
with hourly time resolution [29, 30], deployed in field campaigns in
Hong Kong and Delhi [29, 31]. The same EU directive explicitly names
oxidative potential as a required measurement at monitoring stations —
the first time any major air quality regulation has included it [28].
The remaining obstacle is standardisation: a 2025 interlaboratory
comparison across 20 laboratories found substantial variability in
results between groups using different protocols, and concluded that
harmonisation is a necessary prerequisite before OP data can be
meaningfully compared across networks [32]. Different assays capture
different aspects of oxidative activity, and the field has not yet
agreed on which combination to standardise [33].

**Surface area** is not independently monitored in any regulatory
network. It can be derived from particle size distribution data, which
the new EU directive explicitly requires at monitoring supersites — but
the derivation is a research step, not a reported public metric.

**Chemical composition** requires laboratory analytical techniques that
cannot be miniaturised for real-time field use. It remains valuable for
research and source apportionment, but operates on timescales of weeks
to months from sample collection to result.

In short: particle count has a regulatory deadline. Oxidative potential
has a mandate but needs standardisation. Surface area and composition
remain research-grade. For the two most tractable metrics, the
infrastructure decisions are being made now.

## What Can You Actually Do? 

***[Please read the disclaimer at the end for an accurate interpretation
of this section]:***

The evidence in this piece does not translate into personal risk
calculations — the science does not support that precision. While the
monitoring and measurement technology catches up, there are simple
guidelines you can still refer to, to better protect yourself. A few
things are either consistently supported across the research or are
reasonable implications resulting from it:

-   Route matters more than the city-wide number suggests: taking a
    quieter street over a main road meaningfully reduces exposure to the
    freshest, most reactive particles, regardless of what the AQI says.

-   A well-fitted N95 or KN95 mask reduces PM2.5 inhalation
    substantially during high-pollution periods. Shifting outdoor
    activity away from peak traffic hours reduces exposure in any
    combustion-dominated city.

-   Keeping windows closed during high-pollution events and opening them
    for ventilation when air is cleaner is better than assuming fresh
    air is always better.

-   And running a HEPA air purifier in the room where you sleep — where
    most people spend seven to nine hours — is likely the single most
    direct individual intervention with highest returns.

## **Limitations and What This Piece Can and Cannot Tell You**

The science here is strong in places, early-stage in others. A few
things to keep in mind before drawing conclusions:

The PM2.5-mortality link is one of the most robustly replicated findings
in environmental health. Not contested. The risks of arsenic, cadmium,
PAHs, and black carbon are well-established. The four metrics — mass,
count, surface area, oxidative potential — are real and their variation
across sources is directly supported by the cited studies.

Some findings are well-supported but not definitively proven: the
long-term cardiovascular effects of black carbon in lower-pollution
European settings, and the Beijing cancer risk projections, which are
modelled estimates not measured case counts.

Some are early-stage: neurological effects of air pollution, the HIPTox
trial's cognitive findings with 13 participants, PFAS inhalation health
effects from wildfire smoke specifically, and SOA effects at real-world
concentrations.

Throughout this piece, "associated with" means a statistical
relationship found in a study population — not that pollution caused
disease in any specific person. These are population-level risk
patterns, not individual predictions. Each city's profile is a tendency,
not an exclusive description.

> ***And although 'all PM2.5 is harmful', not all PM2.5 is equally
> harmful.*** In agricultural regions, ammonium sulfate and nitrate
> dominate the PM2.5 mass reading while carrying relatively low
> oxidative potential — a very different situation from diesel or coal
> combustion particles at the same concentration. The strong health
> associations in the literature were built largely on
> combustion-dominated environments, and although they do apply to other
> environments - whether they apply with "equal force" in cleaner
> settings is still being figured out.

## **Conclusion — What the Number Cannot Hold**

We began with a number on an app — checked by millions every morning as
a guide to the air they are about to breathe. That number is the product
of genuine scientific effort and regulatory frameworks that have reduced
pollution and saved lives in many parts of the world.

But a number that only describes weight cannot hold count, surface area,
chemical composition, or the knowledge of where pollution came from.
These are not academic refinements — they are the questions that explain
why identical mass readings in different cities produce different
disease burdens, and why the interventions that actually work are the
ones targeted at what the mass number cannot see.

The four cities in this piece are not edge cases. Delhi-type combustion
pollution affects hundreds of millions across Asia and Africa.
London-type traffic exposure is the daily reality of most dense cities.
Beijing showed that tracking composition — not just mass — is what
allowed policymakers to confirm what they were fixing and which organs
were becoming safer. Los Angeles illustrated that as the nature of what
burns changes, the monitoring frameworks designed for twentieth-century
pollution are increasingly inadequate for twenty-first-century
exposures.

For particle count and oxidative potential, the infrastructure decisions
are being made right now. The gap between what is technically measurable
and what is routinely reported to the public is primarily a question of
regulatory will and data disclosure. For particle count, the science and
instrumentation are ready — it is genuinely a policy question. For
oxidative potential, standardisation of measurement methods across
laboratories is still in progress, so there remains a technical barrier
alongside the regulatory one.

The jar has always contained more than the scale can read. The field is
only now, slowly, learning to look inside it.

## Disclaimer

The information in this piece is provided for general educational and
informational purposes only. It is not intended as, and should not be
construed as, medical advice, clinical guidance, or a substitute for
consultation with a qualified healthcare professional.

The behavioural suggestions in the "What Can You Actually Do?" section
are a set of general advice and may not be appropriate for every
individual. People with pre-existing respiratory conditions (such as
asthma or COPD), cardiovascular disease, or other health conditions;
pregnant women; older adults; children; and others with specific
vulnerabilities may face different risk profiles and benefit from
tailored guidance that this piece cannot provide.

If you have concerns about how air quality may affect your specific
health circumstances, please consult a qualified medical professional.
Air quality conditions vary considerably by location, time, and season —
local public health authorities and healthcare providers are best placed
to give advice relevant to your personal situation.

## Glossary

**PM2.5** — Tiny airborne particles small enough to be inhaled deep into
the lungs. The standard global measure of fine particle air pollution,
expressed as weight per volume of air — micrograms per cubic meter.

**Microgram per cubic meter (μg/m³)** — The unit PM2.5 is measured in.
One microgram is one millionth of a gram. One cubic meter is roughly the
volume of a large wardrobe. A typical grain of table salt weighs around
20 micrograms — so a PM2.5 reading of 60 μg/m³ means the total weight of
all floating particles in that wardrobe-sized volume of air is roughly
equivalent to the weight of 3 grains of salt.

**Aerodynamic diameter** — A way of describing particle size based on
how it moves through air rather than its physical dimensions — used
because real particles are irregular lumps, not neat spheres.

**Ultrafine particles** — Particles smaller than 0.1 micrometers — far
tinier than PM2.5. Not separately regulated. They contribute almost
nothing to the PM2.5 weight reading but can be present in enormous
numbers and penetrate very deep into lung tissue.

**Alveoli** — The tiny air sacs at the deepest part of the lungs where
oxygen passes into the bloodstream and carbon dioxide passes out. Walls
are only one cell thick. Particles that reach here are very difficult
for the body to clear.

**Mucociliary escalator** — The lung's built-in cleaning system. Tiny
hair-like structures lining the airways beat continuously to sweep mucus
— and any trapped particles — upward toward the throat. Works well for
larger particles but cannot catch the smallest ones.

**Oxidative potential** — A measure of how chemically aggressive a
particle is — specifically its capacity to generate reactive oxygen
species on contact with tissue. Independent of particle weight. Varies
enormously depending on what the particle is made of.

**Reactive oxygen species (ROS)** — Highly reactive molecular fragments
produced when certain particles contact biological tissue. They damage
cell membranes, proteins, and DNA. Think of it as a slow chemical
assault on living tissue. A key mechanism linking combustion particle
exposure to cancer and heart disease.

**PAHs (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons)** — A family of toxic organic
compounds formed whenever anything burns incompletely — car engines,
open fires, coal, crop burning. Several are confirmed human carcinogens.
The body's attempt to break them down produces intermediates that damage
DNA directly.

**Black carbon** — The elemental soot core of combustion particles. A
reliable marker of fresh combustion, especially from traffic.
Independently associated with cardiovascular disease beyond what PM2.5
mass alone would predict.

**Agglomerate** — What happens when many tiny fresh particles collide
and stick together in the air, forming a single larger clump. Reduces
particle count and surface area while increasing mass per particle.

**Arterial stiffness** — A measure of how rigid the arteries are.
Stiffer arteries make the heart work harder, which over time is linked
to higher risk of heart attack and stroke. Used as an early indicator of
cardiovascular stress in air pollution research.

**Source apportionment** — The practice of chemically fingerprinting
PM2.5 to work out what fraction came from which source — coal, traffic,
agriculture, industry, and so on. Tells you not just how much pollution
there is, but where it came from.

**PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances)** — A large family of
synthetic chemicals used in non-stick coatings, waterproofing, food
packaging, and firefighting foam. Called "forever chemicals" because
they resist breaking down in the environment or the body. Released when
synthetic materials burn. Their health effects from drinking water
exposure are documented; their specific effects from inhaling wildfire
smoke are not yet well understood.

**BTEX** — Benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylene. Toxic chemicals
released when synthetic materials and fuels burn. Several are confirmed
or probable human carcinogens.

**Organic aerosols** — Airborne particles made primarily of carbon-based
compounds, produced when fuels and organic materials burn incompletely.
High oxidative potential. A major component of PM2.5 in combustion-heavy
cities.

**Ammonium sulfate / ammonium nitrate** — Secondary particles formed
when ammonia from farms and fertilisers reacts with acidic gases in the
atmosphere. They add substantially to PM2.5 mass readings while carrying
relatively low oxidative potential — an example of where a high PM2.5
number does not necessarily mean high toxicity.

**Olfactory nerve** — The nerve responsible for smell, running directly
from the nose to the brain without crossing the blood-brain barrier.
Animal research suggests ultrafine particles may travel along this
pathway into brain tissue, though whether this happens in people
breathing typical outdoor air is still being studied.

**Secondary organic aerosol (SOA)** — Particles that form in the
atmosphere when gases from combustion or consumer products chemically
react with each other, creating new compounds that were not present in
the original emissions. Poorly monitored but a significant fraction of
total PM2.5.

**Wildland-urban interface (WUI)** — Where residential areas meet
wildland vegetation. As housing has expanded into fire-prone land, fires
in these zones have increased in frequency and severity, and their smoke
is chemically more complex than smoke from forest-only fires.
